extracted.intended_audience: maritime historians, shipbuilders, and general readers interested in 19th-century passenger clippers
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive historical account of 19th-century passenger clippers, their design, voyages, captains, and operational practices. Useful for readers studying ship performance, passenger accommodation, and maritime operations of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and performance
rubrics_metrics.description: How fast the ship sailed in different conditions — e.g., "making 300 miles a day", "biggest run in the 24 hours was 336 miles", "fastest speed through the water by the log was 14 knots".
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate using logged runs (24-hour runs, average passage days), recorded top speeds, and comparisons to contemporaneous ships (passing other clippers). Examples: 300 miles/day in easting weather; 14 knots by log; 340 knots in 24 hours cited for Sobraon (note: text sometimes uses 'knots' as 'miles'). Consider both peak runs and averages (e.g., average 74 days Plymouth to Port Adelaide).

rubrics_metrics.name: Light-wind (ghosting) performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability to maintain speed and make way in light airs — the ship's 'ghosting powers' and capacity to pass other clippers when they seemed at anchor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess anecdotal reports of passing other ships in light winds, performance with small sail configurations (e.g., water-sails, flying jib topsails on rivals), and captain/crew testimony about behavior in light airs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sea-keeping and seaworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Qualities that make the ship a good sea boat: 'dry as a bone' decks, fine lines and bows, ability to carry sail and handle heavy weather, and behavior running down easting or on a wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider reports of behavior in easting weather, performance on various points of sail (close-hauled, on the quarter), responses in storms (what canvas was kept), and damage sustained or avoided in heavy seas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: The ship's build and materials — e.g., composite construction of solid teak with iron beams and frames, copper fastening, wrought-iron lower masts, steel topmasts/yards; classing (e.g., 16 years A1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use original construction details to judge strength and longevity (teak + iron framing, copper fastenings, iron/steel spars). Classing and the presence/absence of auxiliary features (skysails, double topgallant yards) inform stability and handling characteristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passenger accommodation and comfort
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision and arrangement for passengers: large first-class saloon (e.g., 200 ft), second-class saloon, fresh food (livestock carried), water condensers, ice chamber, social amenities (fancy dress ball), and not being 'driven' in consideration of passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate size/arrangement of saloons, provisioning (bullocks, sheep, pigs, cows, fowls, condenser/ice), frequency of stops for passengers (St. Helena stay), and operational choices (avoiding hard driving to preserve passenger comfort and health).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety equipment and emergency response
rubrics_metrics.description: Onboard firefighting and lifesaving measures and procedures — e.g., fire extinguishers and hoses used to put out hatch/cargo fires; lifebuoys, quick lowering of boats, man-overboard drills and responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess presence and effectiveness of fire extinguishers/hoses, crew readiness (e.g., 4 minutes to have boat in water after man overboard), documented emergency incidents (coal spontaneous combustion, fires, man overboard) and outcomes, and whether procedures prevented catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reliability and low-damage record
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which the ship avoided serious damage over service life — e.g., 'never had anything approaching a serious loss of spars or sails', 'came through her 25 years' active service with singularly little damage', 'as sound as a bell' on survey.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use log records of lost spars/sails, frequency/severity of repairs, and dry-dock surveys to judge inherent reliability and structural longevity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Command quality and leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: Influence of masters on ship performance and safety — e.g., captain's role in design (Captain H. R. Angel), continual oversight and watchfulness (Captain Elmslie), disciplinary style and its effect on crew and passengers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider length of command, captain's involvement in design/trim, reports of watchfulness and daily attention, crew retention and loyalty, and anecdotes linking captain decisions to reduced incidents or superior voyages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crew continuity, training and morale
rubrics_metrics.description: Length of service and career progression among officers and petty officers, apprentices staying long and becoming masters later — evidence of good management and training (many petty officers served entire careers aboard).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use personnel records (years served, apprentices who became captains) as indicators of stable, well-trained crews that contribute to safe and efficient ship operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage scheduling and routing choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing of sailings (e.g., sailing from England at most favourable time of year), choice of routes for passenger benefit (via Cape and calling at Capetown, St. Helena) or for speed (Backstairs Passage), and monthly line regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate scheduling and route decisions against goals (comfort, publicity, speed). Examples: taking Cape route 'for the benefit of his passengers', or bringing into St. Vincent's Gulf via Backstairs Passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cargo capacity and commercial returns
rubrics_metrics.description: Ship's carrying capacity and its role in revenue (e.g., 'immense carrying capacity', cargo as a good source of revenue; homeward cargo chiefly wool and wheat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess hold capacity, regularity of full loads, cargo mix on outward and homeward runs, and how passenger accommodation traded off against cargo revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance, refit and end-of-life handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Practices and history of refit and repair (put into Pernambuco to refit after dismasting; remasted after fire; Genoese shipbreakers repairing rather than immediately breaking up), and final breaking up after grounding/breaking on rocks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider documented refits, remasting, responses to damage (fire, iceberg strike), shipbreaking decisions based on assessment of model and construction, and the ship's survey condition at end of service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational conservatism when carrying vulnerable passengers
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate choice to avoid hard driving when carrying invalids/consumptives and other vulnerable passengers to ensure health and comfort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note explicit mentions that ships 'were never driven as she might have been' because many passengers were invalids; factor this into evaluations of voyage times vs passenger welfare.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documented incident narratives as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of first-hand letters, captain's reminiscences and apprentices' accounts (e.g., Commander Harry Shrubsole, A. G. Elmslie) to support claims about performance, design choices and incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat contemporary first-hand testimonies, logbook entries and published letters as primary evidence for assessments of speed, seamanship, incidents, and shipboard life.
